study_sequence.directive: State the axioms of a vector space over a field and correctly verify them in standard examples (e.g., F^n, function spaces), distinguishing addition and scalar multiplication.
Define linear combination and span; compute spans in examples; and express the idea of a set generating a vector space or a subspace.
Define linear independence via the unique-zero-coefficients condition; determine dependence/independence in examples; and relate dependence to one vector being in the span of others.

Use the chapter’s results to recognize when a list spans and is independent and thus functions as a basis in examples, emphasizing minimal spanning and maximal independence characterizations (without full dimension theory).
Define subspace and apply the subspace criterion (closure under addition and scalar multiplication) to determine whether a given subset is a subspace, including common counterexamples.
Define sum of subspaces and direct sum; verify when a sum is direct (typically by uniqueness of decomposition or trivial intersection in basic cases); and compute simple decompositions.
Define what a basis is and develop the key results that connect bases to spanning and linear independence, including existence of bases in finite-dimensional spaces.

Define coordinates of a vector relative to a basis and develop how vectors correspond to coordinate tuples (including uniqueness) and how to compute/transform coordinates with respect to a chosen basis.
Define dimension as the length of a basis and state/prove that all bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same length, then use dimension to compare sizes of subspaces and spanning sets.

Produce the central finite-dimensional theorems that bound the size of linearly independent lists by spanning lists (and vice versa), including the replacement/exchange-type arguments used to prove them.
Define quotient spaces V/U, explain cosets and the induced vector-space structure, and connect dimension of V/U to dimensions of V and U in the finite-dimensional case.

State and use dimension relationships involving subspaces (e.g., inequalities and formulas for sums/intersections in finite-dimensional settings) and apply them to determine dimensions of constructed subspaces.
State the definition of a linear map between vector spaces and be able to verify linearity from the defining properties (additivity and homogeneity) in examples.
Produce and apply the statement identifying the range with a quotient of the domain by the null space; use it to relate structure of V and W through T.
Given bases of the domain and codomain, construct the matrix of a linear map and use matrix multiplication to compute images of vectors via coordinate representations.
Define the null space (kernel) of a linear map, compute it in examples, and use it to characterize when a linear map is injective.
Define the range (image) of a linear map, compute it in examples, and use it to characterize when a linear map is surjective.
Define isomorphism/invertible linear map and give criteria (via injective/surjective, kernel/range, or matrix) to decide when a linear map is invertible.
Treat evaluation (at a scalar, or at a linear operator when introduced later) as a linear map and use linear-map ideas (kernel/range) to justify properties of polynomials.
Prove existence/uniqueness of a polynomial with prescribed values at distinct points and construct it (conceptually) using linear-algebra methods.
Define the vector space of polynomials over a field (including the zero polynomial) and the degree function, and show how basic vector-space operations apply to polynomials.
State and use the polynomial division algorithm (quotient and remainder) and extract standard consequences such as uniqueness and degree bounds.
Define the minimal polynomial in the appropriate setting and establish its basic properties that will be used in subsequent chapters on operators.
Connect roots of a polynomial to linear factors, define multiplicity of a zero, and use these ideas to factor polynomials when possible.
Introduce the characteristic polynomial (in the finite-dimensional case) and explain how its roots correspond to eigenvalues, including how it is computed from a matrix representation.
Define algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial and connect it to eigenvalue counting and to limits on dimensions of eigenspaces.
Define the eigenspace corresponding to an eigenvalue, show it is a subspace, and relate its dimension to the number of linearly independent eigenvectors available for that eigenvalue.
Define eigenvalue/eigenvector for a linear operator and explain how to verify them for a given operator or matrix, including basic examples and nonexamples.
State and use criteria for when an operator/matrix is diagonalizable, including the role of having a basis of eigenvectors and how diagonalization changes the matrix form.
Use the minimal-polynomial viewpoint to constrain possible eigenvalues and to relate factorization properties of the minimal polynomial to diagonalizability.
Present the Gram–Schmidt process as a method to turn a linearly independent list into an orthonormal list spanning the same subspace, and specify the conditions under which it works.
Define an inner product (real and complex cases) and the induced norm, and state the core inequalities (Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequality) that make the norm behave like a length.
Introduce the definition and basic properties of the adjoint of a linear map between inner product spaces, emphasizing how it is characterized by the inner product identity.

Connect inner products to linear functionals by showing how every linear functional on a finite-dimensional inner product space can be represented as an inner product with a fixed vector, and state uniqueness.
Define the orthogonal complement of a subspace and describe orthogonal projection onto a subspace, including the key best-approximation/minimization property.
Explain orthogonality, orthonormal sets, and orthonormal bases, including how orthogonality gives linear independence and simplifies coordinate computations.
Define the adjoint T* of an operator T on an inner product space, prove existence/uniqueness in finite dimensions, and practice computing adjoints in coordinates/with respect to orthonormal bases.

State and use definitions (T = T*; TT* = T*T), derive core properties (e.g., real eigenvalues and orthogonality of eigenspaces for self-adjoint; orthogonality relations for normal), and apply these to examples.
Prove and use the real spectral theorem: a self-adjoint operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors; use it to diagonalize and to reason about quadratic forms and orthogonal decompositions.

Define positivity (⟨Tv,v⟩ ≥ 0), relate it to self-adjointness, and establish existence/uniqueness of the positive square root for positive operators, including basic functional-calculus-style consequences in the finite-dimensional setting.
Define unitary operators (T*T = TT* = I) and characterize them via preservation of inner products/norms; connect unitary matrices (in an orthonormal basis) with geometric transformations.
State and use the polar decomposition T = UP (or T = PU) with U unitary and P positive, and explain how it is constructed from (T*T)^{1/2} (or (TT*)^{1/2}) and what parts are unique.

State and use the complex spectral theorem: characterize normal operators via existence of an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (unitary diagonalization), and apply it to analyze structure and compute with such operators.
Explain which operator-structure results require complex scalars (e.g., existence of eigenvalues/triangularization) and provide illustrative contrasts or counterexamples over the reals.
Define p(T) for a polynomial p and operator T, and use polynomial identities (factorization, division) to deduce operator identities, invariant decompositions, and spectral consequences.

Define the minimal polynomial of an operator and prove its existence/uniqueness; derive consequences such as how annihilating polynomials relate to invariant subspaces, eigenvalues, and diagonalizability.

Prove that every operator on a finite-dimensional complex vector space has an upper-triangular matrix with respect to some basis, and use this to read off eigenvalues (diagonal entries) and derive further results.

Develop the notion of generalized eigenvectors and Jordan blocks (or an equivalent Jordan-type decomposition), explaining how the sizes of blocks reflect algebraic/geometric multiplicity and the minimal polynomial.
Prove determinant-based criteria (det(T)=0 iff T not invertible; det(AB)=det(A)det(B)) and connect determinant to eigenvalues/characteristic polynomial when applicable.

Define multilinear maps (linear in each variable separately), give core examples, and prove their basic properties (linearity-in-each-slot consequences, behavior under fixing variables, and composition with linear maps).

Define alternating multilinear forms, state and prove the existence/uniqueness characterization of the determinant as the alternating n-linear map normalized on a basis, and derive standard determinant identities from this characterization.

Develop computational tools (effects of row/column operations, triangular/diagonal cases, expansion formulas) and prove multiplicativity and other key identities connecting determinants to linear maps and matrices.
Introduce the wedge product and alternating tensors/forms, show how alternating multilinear maps factor through exterior powers, and connect this construction to determinants.

Explain how determinant encodes oriented volume scaling of linear maps, including geometric consequences (orientation reversal, absolute value as volume scale) and how this viewpoint recovers algebraic properties.
